chapter_title: Monitoring and Alerting for Debugging with Cloud Monitoring

screens.title: Monitoring and Alerting for Debugging with Cloud Monitoring
screens.subtitle: Design dashboards, craft alerts, track SLOs, and instrument custom metrics for effective debugging

narration.text: In this lesson we will learn how Cloud Monitoring becomes the first line of defense when you debug production systems. You will understand why metrics provide the quick, time-series answers you need — how many requests per second, where latency spikes, and when error rates climb — and how those numerical signals point you to logs and traces for the full story. You'll see practical guidance for designing dashboards that tell a clear story, building alerting policies that reduce noise with multi-condition logic, and using SLOs to protect your error budget before customers are affected. We'll also cover how to collect application-specific data through custom metrics, and how log-based metrics can bridge logs into monitoring. Throughout, expect concrete examples: a web app dashboard showing p99 latency and 5xx error rate, an alert that only fires when error rate and throughput are concurrently high, and an SLO with a burn-rate alert. By the end, you'll be able to choose which metric to watch, how to visualize it, and when to escalate. Think about a recent outage you studied: which single metric would have given you the first early warning? Hold that question as we explore each technique.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Metrics are your quick signal for issues; dashboards make them visible, alerts automate detection, SLOs tie monitoring to reliability, and custom/log-based metrics surface business signals for debugging.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will build in this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design dashboards that communicate application health, craft alerting policies that reduce false positives, define and monitor SLOs to manage error budgets, and implement custom metrics that capture business signals. First, you'll learn to pick the right metrics — the four golden signals — and to arrange them so that a single glance answers whether the system is healthy. Second, you'll practice building alert policies with multiple conditions and notification channels so alerts map to real incidents rather than transient noise. Third, you'll create SLOs and configure burn-rate alerts to get early warnings when reliability is at risk. Finally, you'll instrument custom or log-based metrics so your dashboards reflect the business behaviour most relevant to debugging. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to help you remember the practice, and a verified competency milestone so you know when you have achieved each skill. These competencies prepare you to diagnose issues faster and reduce incident toil in production environments.

screens.title: Practical outcomes and verification
screens.subtitle: What success looks like and how to validate it

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on measurable outcomes and validation steps. Success means dashboards that answer questions instantly, alerts that fire only for service-impacting issues, SLOs that provide early warning through error budget burn, and custom metrics that reflect business events. You'll validate dashboards by checking that p99, throughput, and 5xx charts populate from simulated traffic. You'll validate alerts by simulating error bursts and watching for single-policy notifications instead of floods. For SLOs, success is seeing the burn-rate alert before the SLO violation threshold is reached. For custom metrics, you should be able to push a counter and then filter and group by labels to confirm the data is usable in charts and alerts. A common misconception is assuming more charts mean better monitoring; in practice focused charts keyed to your business flow are more effective. Plan to iterate: adjust aggregations, aligners, and time windows until the same dashboard reliably guides your triage decisions.

keyIdea.title: Verification

screens.title: Metrics, Logs, and Traces — The Observability Trio
screens.subtitle: How each pillar contributes to debugging and why they are complementary

narration.text: Start with a clear definition: metrics are numerical time-series data summarizing system behavior over time, logs are event-level records that provide contextual detail, and traces show the path and timing of individual requests. Metrics tell you what changed — for example a sudden spike in error rate. Logs tell you why by containing error messages and stack traces that explain the cause. Traces tell you where in the request path the latency occurred, often across multiple services. A concrete example: an alert shows 5xx error rate climbing; you open logs and find a specific exception in a service; then you inspect traces to see the downstream call that timed out and caused the exception. A common misconception is treating metrics as sufficient for root cause: they are not. Metrics point you to the problem, but logs and traces complete the investigation. For practical debugging, adopt a workflow: use metrics for detection, logs for diagnosis, and traces for locating the slow or failing call. Keep each pillar instrumented and connected so you can pivot quickly during an incident. How would you change your workflow if a metric alone repeatedly led to false starts?

keyIdea.title: Observability roles
keyIdea.text: Metrics detect, logs explain, and traces locate. Use them together for effective debugging.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.4 › Metrics, Logs, Traces
Definitions
Clear, actionable definitions of each observability pillar and their role during debugging.
Metrics
Numerical time-series that answer what changed and when; used for detection and trending.
Logs
Detailed event records for diagnosing root causes and capturing exception context.
Traces
End-to-end request paths showing latencies and service interactions to find hotspots.
Annotated example workflow
Scenario: 5xx error rate increases for a web service. Steps to debug:
  1. Detect the spike via an error-rate metric alert or dashboard chart.
  2. Open recent logs filtered to the time window to find exception messages and stackframes.
  3. Examine traces for failed requests to identify which downstream call or dependency introduced latency or errors.
  4. Confirm root cause with logs, reproduce locally if possible, and deploy a targeted fix or rollback.
Concrete example
An alert shows error rate rose to 6%. Logs reveal a database connection timeout, and traces show a specific RPC call to the payments service spiking in latency.
Common mistake
Relying only on metrics. Without logs or traces, you will waste time guessing the root cause.
Key Takeaway

Use metrics to detect, logs to diagnose, and traces to locate. Ensure all three are instrumented and linked for rapid debugging.

screens.title: The Four Golden Signals
screens.subtitle: Latency, Traffic, Errors, and Saturation as the core monitoring signals

narration.text: The four golden signals are four categories of metrics that give a compact view of user-facing system health: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Latency measures how long requests take, and using percentiles like p50, p95, and p99 helps you see typical and tail behaviour. Traffic tracks load, for example requests per second or active users. Errors count faulty responses such as 5xx rates. Saturation measures resource pressure, like C P U or queue depth, that limits capacity. A concrete example: if latency increases but traffic is steady and error rate rises, this suggests an internal resource problem rather than a sudden customer surge. A common misconception is over-monitoring low-value metrics; instead pick representative metrics per service and align them to business flows. In practice, combine these signals: an alert might require elevated errors AND high throughput to avoid alerting during low-traffic anomalies. Dashboards should surface these four signals along with key resource metrics to help you quickly isolate whether an issue is user-facing, infrastructure-related, or dependent-service-caused. How would you prioritize which signal to investigate first for an e-commerce checkout flow?

keyIdea.title: Golden signal focus
keyIdea.text: Monitor latency, traffic, errors, and saturation together to detect and classify incidents quickly; use percentiles and business alignment to prioritize.

content.html:
Core Concept › Four Golden Signals
The four golden signals
Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation — the minimal set to start effective monitoring.
Latency
Track p50, p95, p99 to capture normal and tail latency.
Traffic
Requests per second or active sessions measure load on the system.
Errors
Error rate such as 5xx responses indicates failed user requests.
Saturation
Resource utilization and queue lengths that cap throughput.
Concrete scenario
During a flash-sale, traffic doubles and saturation rises. If latency and errors increase only while saturation is high, scaling or throttling is likely the right mitigation. If errors increase without saturation, investigate failure modes or dependency issues.
Key Takeaway

Use the four golden signals as the default dashboard spine and adapt charts per service and business flow.

screens.title: Designing Effective Dashboards
screens.subtitle: Choose metrics, chart types, and organization that tell a clear health story

narration.text: Designing an effective dashboard is both an engineering and storytelling task. Start by selecting the most important metrics for the service and the business flow you care about. Use the four golden signals as anchors, then add resource metrics and key business counters. Choose chart types to highlight patterns: line charts for time series trends and percentiles, heatmaps for distribution over time, and bar charts for categorical breakdowns. Organize the dashboard logically — for example, group charts by user-facing flow, then by infrastructure dependencies. Include summary panels at the top with single-number indicators and recent deltas so an on-call engineer can read status quickly. A concrete example: for a checkout flow include a top-line p99 latency, request throughput, 5xx rate, inventory level, and payment gateway success rate. A common misconception is making dashboards internally focused; always include business metrics so you can relate technical failure to customer impact. Finally, share dashboards with your team and version-control the JSON so changes are auditable and repeatable. Designing Effective Dashboards means start with business-aligned metrics, pick chart types that match the data story, and organize panels for fast triage; keep dashboards focused and shareable.. In practical terms, choose metrics, chart types, and organization that tell a clear health story. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dashboard design
keyIdea.text: Start with business-aligned metrics, pick chart types that match the data story, and organize panels for fast triage; keep dashboards focused and shareable.

content.html:
Process Flow › Dashboard Design
Design steps
  1. Identify key business flows and the metrics that reflect their success.
  2. Pick chart types: percentiles for latency, line for throughput, bar for categorical breakdowns.
  3. Build summary indicators that show current value and recent delta for rapid assessment.
  4. Group panels by service or critical flow, and add dependency sections for infrastructure metrics.
  5. Export dashboard JSON and store in version control for repeatable deployments.
Example: Web App Overview
Top indicators
p99 latency: 320ms • 5xx rate: 0.8% • Throughput: 250 rps
Dependency metrics
DB connections, queue depth, external API success rate — used to triangulate root cause.
Pro tip

Limit dashboard width and keep key indicators above the fold for fast human scanning during incidents.

screens.title: Dashboard JSON and Version Control
screens.subtitle: Export, review, and reuse dashboard definitions as JSON

narration.text: Cloud Monitoring dashboards can be exported as JSON so teams can version, review, and automate dashboard deployment. The JSON contains display names, layout grids, and widget queries. A practical workflow: build the dashboard in the console, export the JSON, store it in your repository, and use automation to apply the dashboard to multiple projects or environments. This ensures consistent observability across testing and production. The JSON example in this chapter shows two widgets: p99 latency and 5xx error rate, each with a time-series query. A common pitfall is editing JSON without understanding the time-series query language or aligners, which may produce misleading charts. Always validate exported dashboards in a staging environment. For teams, a pull-request review of dashboard JSON helps keep the monitoring model consistent. Consider adding a small README next to dashboard JSON explaining the intent of each widget and which alert policies depend on those panels. How will you ensure dashboard changes are tested before deployment? Dashboard JSON and Version Control means export dashboards to json, store in version control, review changes, and automate deployments to keep observability consistent across environments.. In practical terms, export, review, and reuse dashboard definitions as json. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dashboard as code
keyIdea.text: Export dashboards to JSON, store in version control, review changes, and automate deployments to keep observability consistent across environments.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.4 › Dashboard JSON
Export and manage dashboard JSON
Keep dashboard definitions under version control and review changes like any other code.
Example JSON snippet
{
  "displayName": "My Web App Overview",
  "gridLayout": {
    "columns": "2",
    "widgets": [
      {
        "title": "HTTP Request Latency (p99)",
        "xyChart": {
          "dataSets": [
            { "timeSeriesQuery": { "query": "fetch global
| metric 'appengine.googleapis.com/http/server/response_latencies'
| group_by 1m, [value_response_latencies_aggregate: percentile(value.response_latencies, 99)]
| align rate(1m)
| every 1m", "unitOverride": "ms" }, "plotType": "LINE" }
          ]
        }
      },
      {
        "title": "HTTP Error Rate (5xx)",
        "xyChart": { "dataSets": [ { "timeSeriesQuery": { "query": "fetch global
| metric 'appengine.googleapis.com/http/server/response_count'
| filter metric.response_code_class = '5xx'
| group_by 1m, [value_response_count_aggregate: sum(value.response_count)]
| align rate(1m)
| every 1m", "unitOverride": "1" }, "plotType": "LINE" } ] }
      }
    ]
  }
}
Store such JSON in your repo with a short README describing intent, expected data sources, and any alert dependencies so reviewers can reason about impact before approving changes.
Common pitfalls
  • Changing aligners or aggregators in JSON without validation can make charts misleading.
  • Not versioning dashboards leads to divergent monitoring across environments.
Key Takeaway

Treat dashboards as code: export, review, and automate to maintain consistent observability practices.

screens.title: Advanced Alerting Policies
screens.subtitle: Combining conditions and channels to reduce noise and target real incidents

narration.text: Advanced alerting is about precision and actionability. Use multiple conditions combined with logical operators to ensure alerts fire only when an incident truly affects customers. For example, require that error rate exceeds five percent for five minutes AND request throughput is above a baseline. This avoids alerting during low-traffic windows where a few errors are not impactful. Use aggregations and alignment windows to smooth transient spikes. Configure notification channels to match severity: email or chat for low-severity, SMS or PagerDuty for high-severity events where immediate on-call response is required. A concrete setup: a single alerting policy with two conditions, one on a log-based error-rate metric and another on throughput, combined with an AND operator, sending an urgent notification to the on-call rotation. A common misconception is splitting related checks into multiple policies; that creates duplicate notifications. Instead, prefer a single policy with multiple conditions and well-chosen notification routing. Finally, test alert behavior by simulating conditions and confirming a single clear notification reaches the right recipient. Advanced Alerting Policies means combine conditions with logical operators, tune aggregations, and route notifications by severity to reduce noise and ensure actionability.. In practical terms, combining conditions and channels to reduce noise and target real incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Alerting precision
keyIdea.text: Combine conditions with logical operators, tune aggregations, and route notifications by severity to reduce noise and ensure actionability.

content.html:
Core Concept › Advanced Alerting
Alert policy pattern
Create a single alerting policy with multiple conditions and logical operators to avoid alert fatigue.
Example condition set
  1. Error rate (5xx) > 5% for 5 minutes.
  2. Request throughput > baseline threshold for 5 minutes.
  3. Combine with AND so both must be true to trigger.
Notification strategy
Map channels to urgency: Slack or email for informational alerts, SMS or PagerDuty for critical production alerts where immediate on-call action is required.
Test and simulate
Simulate error bursts to confirm the policy triggers once and not multiple times; adjust thresholds and mute windows as needed.
Common mistake
Creating separate policies for related conditions leads to duplicate pages. Use combined conditions instead.
Key Takeaway

Build multi-condition alerting policies and route notifications by severity. Precision reduces noise and focuses responders on real incidents.

screens.title: SLOs, SLIs, and Error Budgets
screens.subtitle: Align reliability targets to customer experience and use error budgets for proactive response

narration.text: Service Level Indicators are carefully defined measurements of service health, such as the percentage of successful HTTP requests or the fraction of requests meeting a latency target. A Service Level Objective is a target for that indicator over a defined period, for example 99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 30 days. The error budget is simply the complement — the allowable unreliability during the compliance period. Monitoring SLOs and watching the error budget burn rate lets you detect when the service is consuming its budget faster than expected. For example, if your 99.9% success SLO allows 0.1% errors, a burn-rate alert set at 2x would notify you when you are consuming budget at twice the acceptable rate in the lookback window, giving you time to act before breaching the SLO. A common misconception is treating SLOs as binary pass/fail; they are an operational tool to prioritize fixes and shape release practices. In practice, SLO-driven alerts change incident response: you focus on slowing burn rather than only reacting after a violation. Consider which business flows should have the strictest SLOs and which can tolerate more error budget.

keyIdea.title: SLO fundamentals
keyIdea.text: SLIs measure, SLOs target, and error budgets quantify allowable unreliability. Use burn-rate alerts to get early warnings.

content.html:
Definition › SLOs & Error Budgets
SLO concepts
Define SLIs carefully, pick a target SLO, and monitor error budget burn to prioritize action.
Example
SLI: request success rate where status code is 2xx. SLO: 99.9% success over rolling 30 days. Error budget: 0.1% of requests may fail during that period.
Burn-rate alert
Set a burn-rate threshold, for example 2x over a one-hour lookback, to warn when budget consumption is rapid.
Operational impact
Using SLOs shifts decision making: you may pause feature launches or reduce risk when error budget burn is high, and focus engineering time where it most improves customer experience.
Key Takeaway

SLOs convert business expectations into operational signals. Watch burn rate to act before an SLO violation occurs.

screens.title: Creating an SLO and Burn-Rate Alert
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: from SLI selection to alerting on error budget consumption

narration.text: Creating an SLO starts with selecting an appropriate SLI and a compliance period. For request-based SLOs choose a clear success definition such as HTTP responses with 2xx status and optionally a latency threshold. Next, choose the performance goal, for example 99.9% over a rolling 30 days, which determines your error budget. In Cloud Monitoring, create the SLO by pointing the good-request numerator to a log-based metric or a direct metric and set total requests as the denominator. Then configure an alerting method: burn rate is common. Set a burn-rate threshold such as 2 and a lookback duration like one hour so you get early warning when error budget is being consumed. A concrete walkthrough from the chapter: create the service named my-web-app, configure the SLI using log-based metrics for good and total requests, set a 99.9% goal, choose rolling 30 days, then add a burn-rate alert with a notification channel for on-call email. A common misconception is to rely on simple threshold alerts only; burn-rate alerts provide a clearer signal about policy risk. After creating the SLO, simulate sustained 5xx errors and observe the SLO dashboard for burn-rate spikes and the corresponding alert.

keyIdea.title: SLO creation steps
keyIdea.text: Select SLI, set SLO target and compliance period, choose burn-rate alert thresholds and lookback windows, then test under simulated errors.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create SLO
Step-by-step
  1. Define SLI: success = JSON log status_code = 200 or metric 2xx count.
  2. Choose SLO target and period, e.g., 99.9% over rolling 30 days.
  3. Create Service and map SLI numerator and denominator to metrics.
  4. Configure burn-rate alert: threshold and lookback (e.g., 2x over 1 hour).
  5. Assign notification channels and test by simulating errors.
Simulation checklist
  • Run simulated error log writes to produce 5xx entries.
  • Wait for log-based metrics to populate and for SLO dashboard to update.
  • Confirm burn-rate alert triggers and notification is received by on-call.
Key Takeaway

SLOs and burn-rate alerts give you early operational signals to act before customer-visible violations occur.

screens.title: Implementing Custom Metrics with OpenTelemetry
screens.subtitle: Instrument application code to publish counters and labels for richer dashboards

narration.text: Custom metrics let you capture business and application-specific signals that built-in metrics do not provide. Using OpenTelemetry or the Cloud Monitoring A P I, instrument your service to emit counters, gauges, or distributions with descriptive labels so you can slice results by region, status, or feature flag. The chapter shows a Python example that configures a MeterProvider and a Google Cloud exporter. The example creates an orders_processed_total counter and increments it with labels like status and region inside the application logic. A concrete example: increment orders_processed_total with status success or failure to track business throughput and error trends in a dashboard. A common mistake is creating high-cardinality labels such as full user IDs; prefer low-cardinality labels like region or status to keep metric storage reasonable. Also choose sensible export intervals; the example uses five-second exports for near-real-time monitoring. After instrumenting, verify the metric appears in Cloud Monitoring and can be used in charts and alert conditions. What business metric from your application would be most useful as a custom metric? Implementing Custom Metrics with OpenTelemetry means instrument with opentelemetry or the api, use low-cardinality labels, set appropriate export intervals, and verify metrics in dashboards and alerts.. In practical terms, instrument application code to publish counters and labels for richer dashboards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Custom metrics practice
keyIdea.text: Instrument with OpenTelemetry or the API, use low-cardinality labels, set appropriate export intervals, and verify metrics in dashboards and alerts.

content.html:
Code Example › Custom Metrics
OpenTelemetry metric snippet
An example that creates a counter and increments it with labels. Validate the metric in Cloud Monitoring after deployment.
from opentelemetry import metrics
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics import MeterProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.metrics.export import PeriodicExportingMetricReader
from opentelemetry.exporter.google_cloud import GoogleCloudMetricExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource

resource = Resource.create({"service.name": "my-order-service"})
metric_reader = PeriodicExportingMetricReader(
  exporter=GoogleCloudMetricExporter(project_id="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"),
  export_interval_millis=5000
)
provider = MeterProvider(resource=resource, metric_readers=[metric_reader])
metrics.set_meter_provider(provider)

meter = metrics.get_meter(__name__)
orders_counter = meter.create_counter(
  name="orders_processed_total",
  description="Total number of orders processed",
  unit="1",
)

# In application logic:
def process_new_order(order_data):
  # ... business logic ...
  orders_counter.add(1, {"status": "success", "region": "us-west1"})
Best practices
  • Use low-cardinality labels like region or status, not unique user IDs.
  • Choose export intervals that balance freshness and cost.
  • Validate the metric in Cloud Monitoring before relying on it for alerts.
Key Takeaway

Custom metrics give you business visibility. Instrument carefully, label sensibly, and verify charts and alerts consume the metric correctly.

screens.title: Using Log-Based Metrics for SLOs
screens.subtitle: Turn structured logs into metrics and use them as SLIs or dashboard signals

narration.text: Log-based metrics bridge logs and metrics by counting or extracting values from structured log entries and converting them into time-series data. This is practical when your application emits structured logs but does not yet have a corresponding metric. The chapter walks through creating two log-based metrics: app_requests_total counting all requests and app_errors_total counting 5xx responses filtered by status_code in the JSON payload. After creating these metrics, you can use them in dashboard charts or as the numerator and denominator for SLO SLIs. A hands-on example: simulate structured logs with gcloud logging write to produce both success and error entries, create the two log-based metrics, then build a dashboard with total requests and error rate. Common pitfalls include using high-cardinality fields in log-based metric labels and expecting immediate data — allow a few minutes for logs to be processed and metrics to appear. Once available, log-based metrics enable quick SLO creation without code changes to emit custom metrics. Using Log-Based Metrics for SLOs means derive time-series from structured logs to create slis and dashboards without changing application code; allow processing time and avoid high-cardinality labels.. In practical terms, turn structured logs into metrics and use them as slis or dashboard signals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Log-based metrics
keyIdea.text: Derive time-series from structured logs to create SLIs and dashboards without changing application code; allow processing time and avoid high-cardinality labels.

content.html:
Process › Log-based Metrics
From logs to metrics
Create counters from structured logs to feed dashboards and SLOs without code changes.
Example log-based counters to create
  1. app_requests_total: Filter by log name for all request entries.
  2. app_errors_total: Filter by log name and jsonPayload.status_code = 500 for error counts.
After creation, use these metrics to build charts or compute an error rate via MQL or by joining numerator and denominator in alerts and SLO definitions.
Hands-on checklist
  • Simulate structured logs with gcloud logging write to populate sample data.
  • Define log-based metrics in Cloud Logging and wait a few minutes for data to appear.
  • Use metrics in dashboard panels and SLO definitions as required.
Key Takeaway

Log-based metrics are a quick path to observability when code changes are not feasible; monitor processing delays and label cardinality.

screens.title: Holistic Observability Strategy for Debugging
screens.subtitle: How dashboards, alerts, SLOs, custom metrics, logs, and traces fit together in practice

narration.text: A holistic observability strategy treats metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, SLOs, and custom metrics as integrated tools rather than separate features. In practice, instrument your services to emit metrics and traces and to write structured logs. Use dashboards to provide quick situational awareness, organize panels by service and business flow, and ensure that each critical flow has an SLO defined. Wire alerts to notify on-call teams with the appropriate urgency and use multi-condition logic to prevent false positives. Produce custom and log-based metrics for business signals like orders processed or inventory level so your dashboards link technical behavior to business impact. For debugging, develop an investigative pattern: start with dashboards to detect anomalies, follow metrics to narrow the window, pivot to logs for details, and inspect traces to find the offending service call. A common mistake is creating isolated dashboards or metrics; instead document dependencies and keep dashboards and alert policies in version control so teams can reproduce and iterate. Finally, run tabletop exercises where simulated errors exercise the entire observability pipeline to validate detection, diagnosis, and response. narration.text: Let's summarize the core ideas to carry forward. First, metrics are time-series numbers that detect issues quickly; they should include the four golden signals for each critical flow. Second, dashboards should be focused and business-aligned so an on-call engineer can assess system health at a glance. Third, advanced alerting uses multiple conditions and proper notification routing to reduce alert fatigue and ensure timely response. Each of these concepts supports quicker detection and more thoughtful escalation. A helpful mental model is: detect with metrics, diagnose with logs, and locate with traces. A common trap is creating noisy alerts or overly complex dashboards. Keep designs simple, measurable, and tied to a clear operational action. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Practical reminders for implementation and practice

narration.text: A few practical reminders will keep your monitoring effective. First, use log-based metrics when adding a new metric by code is impractical; they give quick visibility but may have processing delays. Second, instrument custom metrics with low-cardinality labels and sensible export intervals so your monitoring remains performant and cost-effective. Third, version control dashboard JSON and alert definitions; this makes observability repeatable across projects and easier to review. Always test alerts and SLOs with simulations so you know they behave as intended. A misconception to watch for is trusting raw metric spikes without context; always validate with logs and traces. Finally, practice tabletop exercises to ensure the team understands escalation paths and notification channels. These pragmatic habits turn instrumentation and policies into reliable operational capabilities.
